catalog_citation: Pence, Alan. 1966. Kunimaipa phonology: hierarchical levels. Papers in New Guinea Linguistics 5, Pacific Linguistics A-7: 49-67. Canberra: ANU.
catalog_locator: Section 3 (Phonological Word), 3.1, pp. 52-53 (PDF pp. 4-5); syllable types Section 4, pp. 55-56
catalog_quote: Phonological word (P-word) in Kunimaipa is defined by nuclear stress, CV pattern, timing regularity, and juncture characteristics. 3.1. Placement of the P-word nucleus (and thus stress) is dependent on CV patterns. Each P-word has a nuclear syllable. On words longer than one syllable, this is the syllable closed by the final C; or on P-words which end in a sequence of contiguous V syllables, on the last of those syllables. Stress (heard as slight length or slight intensity, or both) occurs on the nuclear syllable. líƀ 'ashes' lopót 'centre' goulosakár 'both' máop 'owner' maƀáƀo 'red' mutitaé 'pea' nakaí 'near' teteuá 'type of marsupial' Non-contrastive, fluctuating word stresses have been noted on syllables which carry intonational high pitch, following fortis consonants, on low vowels (a, o, e), and on sequences of contiguous vowels. In fast speech these etic stresses tend to disappear…

sources.quote: 'Stress is non-phonemic and occurs usually on penultimate syllable. There is no tone.' (then quotes Pence 1964 on intonation; bibliography cites Pence 1966). Confirms non-contrastive/predictable stress; gives no conditioning. 'Usually penultimate' matches Pence 1966 for the dominant CV-final word shape (and for the vowel-added variants of C-final words, Pence 1966 sec. 3.5) but is in mild tension with Pence's final stress on C-final and VV-final P-words (lopót, goulosakár, mutitaé). A 4-page secondary data sheet; does not override the 1966 analysis.

sources.quote: 'Each I-word has a nuclear contour. In most I-words this occurs on the final syllable; however, an occasional I-word has the nuclear contour spread over two final contiguous vowels... At a P-sentence boundary in distinct or emphatic speech, the nuclear contour sometimes occurs on a final unstressed CV syllable. In the example ... "a boy?", the high nuclear contour occurs on the final syllable whereas the prenuclear contour and P-word nuclear stress occur on the initial syllable...
